articles.title: Cognitive functions relate to the decision-dependent component of football skill in youth academy players
articles.content: Talent identification in football relies increasingly on objective tests. However, these tests capture physical performance better than decision-making, that is, perceiving a game situation and choosing an action. It also remains unclear whether general cognitive functions relate to decision-making on the pitch, partly because studies usually judge skill by playing level or coach ratings, which do not separate decision-making from athletic ability. To address this gap, we tested 79 male academy players aged 12-18 years with a computerized cognitive battery and a football simulator that scores football-specific cognition (decision-making), accuracy, ball control and athletic performance separately. The computerized battery yielded six domain scores: processing speed, executive control, attentional stability, dynamic attention, working memory and cognitive resilience. Processing speed and cognitive resilience correlated with the simulators cognition score, whereas executive control and working memory did not. An overall cognitive score correlated with accuracy, the decision-dependent component, but not with athletic performance. Exploratory analyses located this association mainly in passing accuracy. The six cognitive domains explained an additional 22% of the variance in accuracy beyond age, and athletic performance. Therefore, cognitive functions were associated with the decision-dependent component of objectively measured skill, not with its athletic component, which supports adding targeted cognitive tests to academy assessment batteries.
articles.author: Czeszumski, A., Ludwiczak, M., Kolff, K., Grzadzielewski, J., Jasinska, J., Hirsch, K., Nezami, F. N.

articles.title: Chewing-related changes in ankle muscle activity and spectral power are modulated by oral anesthesia during single-leg stance
articles.content: Mastication can facilitate lower-limb motor output, yet whether its influence on postural muscle control depends on oral sensory feedback is unknown. In a randomized, placebo-controlled, parallel-group study, 27 healthy adults performed sub-maximal single-leg stance trials at baseline, after unilateral buccal lidocaine (n = 12) or placebo (n = 15) spray, and while chewing gum. Center-of-pressure sway and surface electromyography of the tibialis anterior (TA) and medial gastrocnemius (GM) were analyzed during the first 3 s of unipedal support. Sway area showed no significant Group, Block, or interaction effects. Group differences emerged only in the change from spray alone to chewing: GM amplitude increased overall, whereas TA amplitude increased only with placebo and TA-GM coactivation only under anesthesia (Group-by-Block interactions). An exploratory cluster-based analysis, at the threshold of significance, showed greater chewing-related increases in TA spectral power (20-200 Hz) under anesthesia, early after stance onset. Participants with larger chewing-related TA power increases, most robustly at 40-80 Hz, showed smaller proportional changes in sway area, and greater trial-level TA power accompanied smaller mediolateral sway. These findings suggest that oral anesthesia alters how mastication engages early ankle neuromuscular control, revealing subtle adjustments not evident in sway area.
articles.author: Jimenez-Zuniga, S., Espinoza, S., El-Deredy, W.

articles.title: Baseline Predictors of Craving Reduction Following Non-Invasive Neuromodulation: A Computational Modeling Approach
articles.content:
BackgroundAlcohol craving is a clinically relevant symptom with an established neurobiological basis and has emerged as a treatment target. Non-invasive neuromodulation has shown potential for reducing craving, but substantial inter-individual variability in response is a pervasive challenge. This study examined whether baseline computational parameters predicted treatment response following neuromodulation.

MethodsThis secondary analysis of an open-label, randomized trial included 58 individuals with subclinical alcohol use who received transcutaneous auricular vagus nerve stimulation (taVNS), transcranial photobiomodulation (tPBM), or combined taVNS + tPBM for five weeks. Baseline computational measures from Delay Discounting, Choice under Risk and Ambiguity, and Loss Aversion Tasks were examined as predictors of treatment response. Elastic net regularization was used to identify markers associated with Reliable Change Index (RCI)-defined responder status, alongside demographic variables, intervention condition, and baseline craving.

ResultsOf the 58 participants, 24 were classified as treatment responders. The elastic net model showed a mean test AUC of 0.66 across 1,000 iterations, indicating modest predictive performance. Baseline craving, intervention condition, age, sex, and computational modeling parameters contributed to responder status: Higher loss aversion and lower risk sensitivity were associated with a greater likelihood of responder status.

ConclusionsBaseline computational measures, particularly loss aversion and risk sensitivity, may serve as candidate behavioral markers associated with craving reduction following non-invasive neuromodulation. Given the open-label design, these findings represent an initial proof-of-concept. Future sham-controlled studies are needed to determine whether these parameters are associated with stimulation-specific responses or more general susceptibility to behavioral change.

Clinical trial registrationThe trial was registered at ClinicalTrials.gov (NCT07071493).
articles.author: Kang, J., Choi, J.-S., Jung, Y.-C., Kim, M., Park, M., Kwon, M., Lee, Y., Chung, D.-i., Ahn, W.-Y.

articles.title: Domain-general and domain-specific neural mechanisms underlie metacognition in social and perceptual decisions
articles.content: Metacognition, the monitoring and assessment of our own cognitive processes, plays a key role in our everyday decision-making across a multitude of domains. Despite this, the question of whether metacognition is implemented by domain-general or domain-specific neural processes has not yet been conclusively answered. Theoretical two-layer accounts propose that a shared core network of metacognition, consisting of prefrontal areas, might be functionally coupled with task-relevant brain regions in a domain-specific way. To test this empirically, the present study comprises three experiments. In the first experiment, participants underwent neuroimaging to compare the neural correlates of metacognitive judgements in a novel social decision task with those in an established perceptual decision task. Prefrontal areas, such as FPC, dmPFC, and dlPFC, showed domain-general activations associated with confidence, while connectivity of the FPC with task-related regions (TPJ vs. occipital cortex) was correlated with metacognition in a domain-specific way. In two further experiments, participants performed the same two tasks, while tACS was applied to selectively modulate connectivity between FPC and the TPJ or the occipital cortex, aiming to test whether this connectivity causally underlies metacognition. Indeed, the results suggest that altering FPC-TPJ vs. FPC-occipital cortex connectivity had domain-specific effects on metacognition. Together, our findings provide evidence for both domain-specific and domain-general neural mechanisms of metacognition, aligning with theoretical two-layer accounts, and advancing our understanding of the nature of metacognitive processes in different domains.
articles.author: Mattes, R. S., Vural, G., Drexler, S., Xia, H., Deroy, O., Soutschek, A.

articles.title: Genetic Influence on the Sleep EEG is Distributed Across Multiple Traits
articles.content: Sleep spindles are among the most promising neurophysiological biomarkers in sleep research: they support memory consolidation, track healthy aging, are altered in psychiatric, neurodevelopmental, and neurodegenerative disorders, and are highly trait-like, varying between individuals while remaining stable within them across nights. Twin studies have shown that conventional spindle features such as density, amplitude, and duration are heritable, but important aspects of spindle activity remain unstudied, including spindle coupling to the slow-oscillation phase, which supports memory consolidation, and the individualized timing patterns that dominate spindle production. Spindles are also only a subset of a broader class of transient oscillations spanning 2-16 Hz that are more stable across nights than conventionally detected spindles and are altered in disorders such as schizophrenia, and whose genetic basis is unknown. Addressing these gaps is difficult because twin cohorts are small, which limits the detection of modest genetic effects one trait at a time. We analyzed sleep EEG (C3/C4) from 47 monozygotic (MZ) and 32 dizygotic (DZ) same-sex twin pairs (mean age 26.9{+/-}6.4 years). The DYNAM-O toolbox characterized transient oscillatory peaks in N2/N3 sleep, yielding 32 traits: event features in four frequency bands, fast-spindle timing patterns, and relative spectral power. MZ-DZ differences in intraclass correlation (ICC) were tested trait by trait with permutation tests (100,000 permutations, false discovery rate (FDR) correction) and jointly with group tests and multivariate co-twin distance. Fast-spindle (11-16 Hz) duration (ICC: MZ 0.82 vs DZ 0.31), prominence (0.81 vs 0.38), and slow-oscillation power (0.55 vs -0.10) showed greater MZ than DZ resemblance, as did the previously unstudied fast-spindle refractory period (0.68 vs 0.16) and the slow-oscillation power of 9-11 Hz and 5-9 Hz events (all FDR-adjusted p[≤]0.048). Preferred slow-oscillation phase showed no MZ-DZ difference in any band. Joint tests were more sensitive than any single trait: across all 32 traits, MZ co-twins were closer than DZ co-twins (0.86 vs 1.14, p=0.00002) and the mean-Z test was highly significant (p=0.00009), whereas the strongest single trait, corrected for the number of traits tested, was not (p=0.10). Genetic influence on sleep EEG therefore extends beyond fast spindles to lower-frequency transient oscillations and spindle timing, and is distributed across many traits in a pattern that single-trait analyses understate, supporting multivariate sleep biomarkers.
articles.author: Saremsky, S. R., Chen, S., Staley, B., Pack, A. I., Purcell, S. M., Prerau, M. J.

articles.title: The entorhinal elliptic frame: emergence and persistence of coherent neural representations across contexts as Mordell-Weil sections
articles.content: Entorhinal grid-cell recordings reveal toroidal population activity across environments even as spatial firing maps shift, rescale, and shear. What geometric structure couples cue-evoked phases across contexts, and how can cross-context coherence fail while local toroidal coding remains intact? Extending recent computational accounts of latent oscillatory dynamics in the medial temporal lobe, we introduce the entorhinal elliptic frame (EEF). The EEF models grid-module state tori over calibrated contexts as a holomorphic family and assumes that this family extends to a Jacobian elliptic surface over a context Riemann sphere. Global holomorphic sections represent coherent cue profiles, and deformation of the surface models slow plasticity. For every surface height n [≥] 3 and every 1 [≤] r [≤] 10, surfaces of exact Mordell-Weil rank r are analytically dense among simply-branched surfaces with only nodal singular fibers. A transverse tuple of r independent sections persists on a locus of complex dimension 10n - 2 - r(n - 1), which measures the compensatory reserve. For ten such sections, this persistence locus has complex dimension eight at every surface height n [≥] 2. If nine complex Schiffer coordinates are frozen, almost every sufficiently small prescribed offset obstructs simultaneous continuation of the tuple to nearby surfaces. In synthetic spike benchmarks with known conformal fiber shapes and marked phase axes, a Cauchy-Riemann assay distinguished equal-magnitude holomorphic and antiholomorphic cue displacements on a fixed torus and on a smooth patch of a height 10 surface, while free-exploration spikes retained a torus-compatible signature under both fixed-torus cue rules. Our model predicts a functional dissociation under progressive loss of plasticity. Once compensatory reserve is exhausted, local toroidal coding can remain intact even when a chosen set of coherent cue profiles can no longer persist together as the architecture changes.
articles.author: Park, J.-Y., Jones, D. T., Breakspear, M.

articles.title: Ketamine reverses chronic corticosterone-induced changes in dendritic spine morphology in hippocampal but not cortical neurons in vitro
articles.content: Chronically elevated glucocorticoids, such as corticosterone (CORT), reduce dendritic spine density in the prefrontal cortex and hippocampus, and the rapid-acting antidepressant ketamine (KET) reverses this spine loss in the prefrontal cortex. Less is known about how CORT affects spine morphology, whether these effects differ between the cortex and hippocampus, and whether KET counteracts them. Most studies used stress models or systemic CORT, making it difficult to distinguish direct and indirect effects of CORT on neurons. We therefore used primary mouse cortical and hippocampal cultures, which isolate these direct effects. We found that chronic CORT (0.25 M, 72 h) altered spine morphology differently in each culture. In cortical neurons, CORT narrowed spine heads and increased the length-to-head-width ratio, and the selective glucocorticoid receptor (GR) modulator CORT108297 abolished the CORT-induced narrowing of spine heads. By contrast, in hippocampal neurons, CORT reduced spine length, head width, and spine area, making dendritic spines proportionally smaller. Because dendritic spine structure and network activity shape each other, we also recorded spontaneous Ca2+ activity. The regional divergence observed in spine structure also extended to network activity: CORT shortened the intervals between Ca2+ events in hippocampal but not in cortical cultures. KET (10 M, 24 h) did not counteract CORT effects in cortical cultures, whereas in hippocampal cultures it reversed the CORT-induced reduction in spine size. In both cultures, KET reduced network synchronization independently of CORT. Thus, CORT remodels dendritic spines in a region-specific manner, and KET counteracts its effects on spine morphology only in hippocampal neurons.
articles.author: Wilczkowski, M., Kaczek, K., Chmielarz, P., Mieszczak, P., Gorka, K., Alwani, A., Zelek-Molik, A., Nalepa, I.

articles.title: Network Correlates of Shared Experience in Musical Improvisation
articles.content: Shared experiences emerge when individuals feel attuned to one another as they coordinate their actions and mental states, constituting a fundamental part of everyday human life. Yet, the neural mechanisms underpinning these phenomena remain poorly understood. Musical improvisation provides an ecologically valid setting for studying shared experiences, as it combines creativity, joint action, and real-time adaptation. Here, we investigate the neural correlates of shared experience during group musical performance using hyperscanning EEG recordings of professional musicians performing in naturalistic settings in front of an audience. Musicians performed each piece under two conditions: a strict rendition, focused on precise execution of the score, and a letgo version, which encourages improvisation and risk-taking. This approach enables the isolation of neural signatures specifically associated with improvisational and shared states of mind, which we probe using tools from information theory and network science. Our results reveal that, across most pieces and ensembles, letgo performances are associated with greater signal complexity and interdependence within and between brains, alongside denser, more cohesive information flow and a more synergistic combination of the musicians' brain networks. These findings point to more integrated collective neural dynamics during letgo, consistent with the emergence of a shared experience, and suggest that neural signatures of conscious states may extend beyond individual brains to interacting systems. Beyond these empirical findings, this work introduces a methodological toolkit combining complexity measures, higher-order information-theoretic metrics, and network-based analyses to investigate inter-brain coordination and collective cognition in naturalistic settings.
articles.author: Liardi, A., Sas, M. I., Rajpal, H., Bratu, I.-F., Rosas, F. E., Mediano, P. A. M., Jensen, H. J.

articles.title: Microscopic Elementary Current Properties Survive Across Scales Shaping Spectral And Non-Linear Features Of Field Potentials
articles.content: The temporal fluctuations of field potentials (FPs) carry information about upstream neuronal dynamics, but their extracellular expression is shaped by the anatomo-functional properties of the receiving population. Inferring upstream dynamics from FPs requires understanding how incoming activity is transformed by the receiving population. We here explored whether elementary synaptic current waveform shape contributes to mesoscopic fluctuations or is diluted during micro-to-mesoscopic integration. Using spatially stable hippocampal FP generators as templates for reconstruction provided pathway-specific temporal fluctuations while avoiding the ambiguities introduced by source geometry and mixing in raw FPs. Long epochs encompassing diverse temporal patterns helped identify general effects of elementary current properties. Synaptic-like unitary extracellular contributions (UECs) with prescribed waveforms were introduced, keeping the temporal sequence of microscopic events identical to isolate their impact on mesoscopic properties. UEC waveform shape influenced mean mesoscopic DC-like amplitude and both readily observable FP properties (amplitude, waveform and spectral composition) and less directly observable, predominantly non-spectral features captured by nonlinear, fractal and entropy-based measures. These effects were generator-specific, yet largely consistent across animals and independent surrogate event trains extracted from the original patterns. Thus, population integration does not erase the influence of elementary extracellular current properties, but transforms how they are expressed in mesoscopic FP features. These findings suggest that, in addition to upstream output patterns, postsynaptic contributions also shape both readily observable and less directly observable FP features, and that different pathways may contribute differently according to the properties of their elementary postsynaptic currents.
articles.author: Munoz-Arnaiz, R., Ramirez-Frias, A., Ashouri, F., Makarova, J., Herreras, O.

articles.title: Isoflurane Anesthesia under Hyperoxic Conditions Shapes Cortical Hemodynamics and Photothrombotic Injury Severity in Mice: A Wide-Field Optical Imaging Study
articles.content: Background/Objectives: Anesthesia can alter cortical hemodynamics and the severity of experimental brain injury. We investigated how isoflurane under hyperoxic conditions affects these. Methods: Wide-field optical imaging (WFOI) in light-scattering mode (505 and 656 nm) through a chronic cranial window was used to assess hemoglobin dynamics in awake (n = 9) and isoflurane-anesthetized (n = 7) mice with intact cortices. Injury was assessed over 3 days after awake photothrombosis (Awake PT, n = 5), anesthetized photothrombosis (1.5% isoflurane/98.5% oxygen; IsO2 PT, n = 7), or laser irradiation without effective intravenous photosensitizer delivery (post hoc Laser group, n = 6). Assessments included FITC-dextran imaging of microcirculation and blood-brain barrier permeability, sensorimotor and biochemical tests, and 2,3,5-triphenyltetrazolium chloride (TTC) staining. Anesthesia induction was studied separately (n = 6). Results: Anesthesia increased relative power at 0.05-0.10 Hz (p = 0.022) and primary motor cortex homotopic connectivity (p = 0.010), while reducing retrosplenial-sensorimotor correlations (p = 0.027). Anesthesia induction increased cortical blood oxygenation and total hemoglobin concentration. Mean lesion areas, early homotopic connectivity loss, day-1 forelimb asymmetry, and day-3 serum neuron-specific enolase increases followed a severity gradient (Laser < Awake PT < IsO2 PT). WFOI-derived lesion areas across the three groups at 10 min after irradiation were 2.03 {+/-} 0.99, 3.54 {+/-} 1.58, and 6.24 {+/-} 1.36 mm2 (overall p < 0.001); day-3 TTC-negative areas were 1.60 {+/-} 0.73, 4.81 {+/-} 2.03, and 10.75 {+/-} 1.61 mm2, respectively. IsO2 PT showed greater microvascular blockage, blood-brain barrier leakage, and approximately twofold longer hemodynamic responses to spreading depolarizations (p = 0.017) than Awake PT. Conclusions: Isoflurane anesthesia under hyperoxic conditions affects baseline cortical activity and exacerbates photothrombotic injury, potentially through enhanced oxygen-dependent photochemistry, emphasizing the importance of anesthetic regimens in experimental models.
